title: Japan's Newspaper Subscription Rate Falls Below 50%
paragraphs: The percentage of people in Japan who have a monthly subscription to a newspaper has fallen below 50% for the first time, according to a new survey.
The Japan Press Research Institute surveyed almost 2,700 people across the country in July and August this year, asking people how they use and feel about different types of media.

The results showed that the newspaper subscription rate has fallen to 49.8% — down from 50.1% last year. The subscription rate has been falling steadily since the survey was first done in 2008, when the rate was 88.6%.

Since 2008, the subscription rate for national newspapers such as The Asahi Shimbun and The Yomiuri Shimbun has fallen the most, going down 33.7 percentage points to 21.4%. However, the rate for prefectural and local newspapers has only fallen 6.4 percentage points over that time, and is actually up a little this year, to 21.2%.
This year, the share of survey participants who said they get their news from newspapers also fell below 50% for the first time, to 49.7%.

People are most likely to get their news from commercial TV stations, named as a regular news source by 84.2% of survey participants. The internet was named by 74.4%, while the TV news shows of Japan's public broadcaster, NHK, were named by 69.7%. Just 27.6% of people said they get their news from the radio.
Survey participants were also asked to give different news sources a score between 0 and 100 according to how much they trust them.

NHK TV got the highest trust score, with 66 points. Newspapers came second with 65 points, and commercial TV was third with 60 points. Radio was in fourth place with 54 points, and the internet got the lowest level of trust, with 47 points.
